title: The Z-Transform
intro: The z-transform turns a list of samples x[n] into a function X(z) on the complex plane. This topic reads it as a landscape: a surface standing over the plane, held up by poles, pinned down by zeros, and cut along the unit circle to give the frequency response.

blocks.text: A discrete-time signal is a list of numbers $x[n]$, one for each whole number $n$. The z-transform packs the whole list into a single function of a complex variable $z$:

Every value of $z$ is a point in the complex plane, so $X(z)$ gives a complex number at every point. Its size $|X(z)|$ is a height, and plotting that height above the plane gives a surface. Almost everything about the z-transform can be read off that surface:

items: Poles are where the surface shoots up to infinity, like tent poles holding up a canvas.
Zeros are where it touches the floor, $X(z) = 0$.

The region of convergence (ROC) is the part of the plane where the sum actually adds up to a finite number. Outside it the formula still gives a surface, but the sum it came from does not exist there.
The unit circle $|z| = 1$ is where the z-transform becomes the frequency response. Walking round it and reading the height gives how strongly each frequency passes.
Whether a system is stable or causal is a question about where the ROC sits relative to the unit circle and the poles.

blocks.text: The viewer below draws that surface for eleven input signals. Pick one from Input signal, then press Next step ▶ to walk through it in eight steps: the samples, the sum, the poles and zeros, the surface, the ROC, the unit circle, reading the height with a ruler, and stability and causality. The panel that each step is about is outlined.

items: Drag the 3D view to turn it, or use Turn and Tilt. A tilt near 85° looks straight down and turns the surface into a contour map of the pole-zero plot.
Radius r and Angle θ move the poles and zeros of the signals that use them (the readout says when a signal ignores one).

Probe frequency ω moves the red point round the upper half of the unit circle. The z-plane panel draws a green line from every zero and a dashed violet line from every pole to it; the response panel marks the same frequency. Sweep ω moves it for you.
Height shows switches between decibels, $20\log_{10}|X(z)|$, which makes zeros into deep pits and keeps poles in view, and the plain magnitude $|X(z)|$, which shows how sharp a resonance really is.
Solid colour is inside the ROC, faded colour outside it. The shaded ring in the z-plane panel is the ROC from above.

blocks.text: The surface in decibels is clipped at +30 dB and −30 dB, so a pole appears as a flat plateau and a zero as a flat-bottomed pit. Mathematically the pole goes to infinity and the zero to minus infinity in decibels.

items: Points of the z-Plane (#/math/z-transform/z-plane): what $z^{-n}$ does to a sample, as a spiral, and why some circles make the sum converge.
The Surface |X(z)| (#/math/z-transform/surface): factoring $X(z)$ into poles and zeros, and why that fixes the whole landscape.
The Region of Convergence (#/math/z-transform/region-of-convergence): rings, right-sided and left-sided signals, and two signals with the same formula.
The Unit Circle and Frequency Response (#/math/z-transform/unit-circle): slicing the surface along $|z| = 1$, and reading the response with a ruler.
Pole Positions and the Time Signal (#/math/z-transform/poles-and-time): how far out a pole sits sets the decay, its angle sets the oscillation, and stability follows.
Properties as Geometry (#/math/z-transform/properties): delay, scaling, modulation, time reversal and convolution as moves of the plane.
Inverting the Transform (#/math/z-transform/inverse): getting $x[n]$ back, by partial fractions or by integrating round a circle.
A Gallery of Signals (#/math/z-transform/gallery): every signal in the viewer, walked through from sequence to stability.
Z-Transform Tables (#/math/z-transform/tables): pairs, properties and one-sided rules to look up.

blocks.text: Complex numbers in polar form, $z = \rho e^{j\omega}$, and the geometric series $\sum_{n\ge 0} a^n = 1/(1 - a)$ for $|a| < 1$. This topic writes the imaginary unit as $j$, as engineers do; mathematicians write $i$. The library's page Complex Numbers (#/quantum/foundations/complex-numbers) covers the polar form.

items: Alan V. Oppenheim and Ronald W. Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing, 3rd edition (Pearson, 2010), chapter 3, The z-Transform.
John G. Proakis and Dimitris G. Manolakis, Digital Signal Processing: Principles, Algorithms, and Applications, 4th edition (Pearson, 2007), chapter 3.

Julius O. Smith III, Introduction to Digital Filters with Audio Applications (W3K Publishing, 2007; free online at ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters), the chapters Transfer Function Analysis and Pole-Zero Analysis.
